terms.definition: The moment a neuron's dendrites detect an incoming signal — chemical, mechanical, or electrical — and the membrane begins to depolarize.
terms.function: Starts the whole nerve-signaling chain by converting an outside trigger (heat, touch, light, or a chemical from another neuron) into the beginning of an electrical response.
terms.whereItIs: The branching dendrite tips of the presynaptic neuron, where 3-4 branches converge toward the cell body.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a clear starting trigger, a neuron has nothing to pass along — this is the step that turns the outside world into a nervous-system signal.

terms.definition: The stage where the action potential propagates rapidly down the myelinated axon, jumping between exposed nodes of Ranvier.
terms.function: Carries the signal at high speed from the cell body all the way to the axon terminals using saltatory conduction along the myelin-insulated shaft.
terms.whereItIs: Mid-shaft of the axon, centered on a gap (node of Ranvier) between two myelin sheath segments.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the step that gives nerve signals their speed — without myelin and saltatory conduction, reflexes and thoughts would happen far too slowly to be useful.

terms.definition: The stage where the arriving impulse triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the axon terminal membrane and release neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft.
terms.function: Converts the electrical signal into a chemical one so it can cross the gap between two neurons that don't physically touch.
terms.whereItIs: One of the bulbous axon terminal boutons at the end of the presynaptic neuron, just before the synaptic cleft.
terms.whyItMatters: This chemical hand-off is the reason so many medicines (painkillers, antidepressants, anesthesia) work — they all act by changing what happens at this exact step.

terms.definition: The stage where neurotransmitter molecules cross the synaptic cleft and bind receptors on the postsynaptic neuron's dendrite, triggering a new electrical signal in that cell.
terms.function: Restarts the electrical signal in the next neuron in the chain, continuing the message onward.
terms.whereItIs: The receiving dendrite/soma surface of the postsynaptic neuron, directly across the synaptic gap from the presynaptic terminal boutons.
terms.whyItMatters: Every hand-off has to succeed for a signal to travel any distance — this is the step that makes a chain of separate cells behave like one continuous pathway.

terms.definition: The final stage where the signal reaches an effector — a muscle or gland — and produces a physical response such as contraction or secretion.
terms.function: Turns the nervous system's electrical/chemical message into a visible, physical action in the body.
terms.whereItIs: The stylized effector-tissue block positioned downstream of the postsynaptic neuron, representing the end organ.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the payoff step — it's why nerve signaling matters at all: flinching off a hot stove, catching a ball, and every other reflex or voluntary movement ends here.

terms.definition: A nerve cell specialized to receive and send electrical and chemical signals.
terms.function: Acts as the basic messenger unit of the nervous system, chaining together with other neurons to carry signals over distance.
terms.whereItIs: Throughout the brain, spinal cord, and nerves; two neurons (presynaptic and postsynaptic) appear in this model on either side of the synapse.
terms.whyItMatters: Nerve signaling is simply what a neuron does — understanding the cell (see the Neuron component in Cell Biology) is the foundation for understanding this process.

terms.definition: Anything that triggers a response in the body, like heat, light, sound, or pressure.
terms.function: Provides the initial trigger that a neuron's dendrites detect, kicking off the signaling chain.
terms.whereItIs: Outside the neuron — it can originate from the environment (a hot stove) or from another neuron's chemical signal.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a stimulus, there is nothing for the nervous system to respond to.

terms.definition: The long, thin, tail-like part of a neuron that carries the electrical impulse away from the cell body.
terms.function: Provides the physical pathway the electrical impulse travels along on its way to the axon terminals.
terms.whereItIs: Running from the presynaptic neuron's cell body to its terminal boutons, wrapped in myelin sheath segments.
terms.whyItMatters: The axon's length and insulation determine how far and how fast a single neuron can send a signal.

terms.definition: The tiny gap between two neurons (or a neuron and a muscle) where the signal crosses using chemicals.
terms.function: Separates two neurons so the signal must convert from electrical to chemical and back, which lets the nervous system control, strengthen, or weaken signals between cells.
terms.whereItIs: The visible gap between the presynaptic neuron's axon terminal boutons and the postsynaptic neuron's dendrite surface.
terms.whyItMatters: Synapses are where learning, memory, and most nervous-system medicines actually happen — they are not just a passive gap.

terms.definition: A chemical messenger released at the synapse that carries the signal to the next cell.
terms.function: Diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the next cell, chemically continuing a signal that can't jump the gap electrically.
terms.whereItIs: Released from synaptic vesicles inside the axon terminal boutons into the synaptic cleft.
terms.whyItMatters: Neurotransmitters are how caffeine, many medicines, and neurological conditions change the way neurons communicate.

terms.definition: A fatty insulating layer wrapped around many axons that speeds up signal travel.
terms.function: Insulates segments of the axon so the electrical signal jumps quickly between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier) instead of leaking away.
terms.whereItIs: Wrapped in discrete segments around the axon shaft, with small gaps between segments.
terms.whyItMatters: Myelin is why some signals travel over 100 meters per second — damage to it, as in multiple sclerosis, slows reactions and can cause numbness.

terms.definition: A small, exposed gap in the myelin sheath along an axon where the axon membrane is uninsulated.
terms.function: Lets the electrical impulse regenerate at each gap, which is what makes saltatory conduction possible.
terms.whereItIs: The narrow gaps between adjacent myelin sheath segments along the axon.
terms.whyItMatters: Nodes of Ranvier are the reason myelinated axons conduct signals so much faster than bare, unmyelinated ones.

terms.definition: The way an electrical impulse appears to "jump" rapidly from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier along a myelinated axon, instead of traveling continuously.
terms.function: Speeds up impulse conduction dramatically compared to an unmyelinated axon of the same width, since the impulse only has to regenerate at the exposed nodes.
terms.whereItIs: Occurs specifically along myelinated stretches of the axon, jumping between nodes of Ranvier.
terms.whyItMatters: Saltatory conduction is the main reason myelinated neurons can send signals fast enough for split-second reflexes and coordinated movement.

terms.definition: A fast-moving wave of electrical change (also called an action potential) that travels down the axon.
terms.function: Carries the neuron's signal from the cell body to the axon terminals as a self-propagating electrical event.
terms.whereItIs: Travels along the length of the axon, from the cell body to the terminal boutons.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the electrical half of nerve signaling — it's what makes nerve signals fast compared to purely chemical communication in the body.

terms.definition: A protein on the next neuron's surface that catches a specific neurotransmitter, like a lock catching a key.
terms.function: Binds a matching neurotransmitter and triggers a new electrical response in the receiving cell.
terms.whereItIs: Embedded in the postsynaptic neuron's membrane, facing the synaptic cleft.
terms.whyItMatters: Receptors determine which neurotransmitters a cell can actually respond to — this specificity is why different chemical messengers have very different effects.

terms.definition: A brief period right after a neuron fires during which it resets its electrical balance before it can fire again.
terms.function: Prevents a neuron from firing continuously without pause and helps keep signals traveling in one direction.
terms.whereItIs: Occurs along the axon immediately after an electrical impulse has passed through a given section.
terms.whyItMatters: The refractory period is why nerve signals are brief, distinct pulses rather than one continuous current, which keeps information encoded clearly.
